## What the data actually shows

**Historical averages (2025‑01‑01 through 2026‑06‑30, from `crm_leads` + `jobs` + `ledger`):**

- **Channel A:** 338 leads (67 won, 271 lost) → 19.8% conversion. Job contribution (revenue − direct cost) = $33,249.65. Ad spend = $6,000 total over the period ($1,000/quarter, flat for all 6 quarters). Net = $27,249.65 → **≈$80.62 net contribution per lead**.
- **Channel B:** 161 leads (64 won, 97 lost) → 39.8% conversion. Contribution = $36,948.22. Ad spend = $4,800 total ($800/quarter, flat for all 6 quarters). Net = $32,148.22 → **≈$199.68 net contribution per lead**.

Those are lower than the $70/$250 you quoted, but they point the same way: B is roughly 2.5x more profitable per lead than A on the history we have. So the "B is the better channel" conclusion is well supported.

## Why I can't tell you what the extra $800 brings in

I pulled the actual spend ledger. Channel B's spend has been **exactly $800/quarter for all six quarters on record** — it has never moved. Same for Channel A at a flat $1,000/quarter. There is no quarter in this business's history where B spend was higher or lower than $800, so there is no data point anywhere showing how leads respond when spend changes.

Making this worse: lead volume for B swung from 23 to 40 leads/quarter even while spend stayed flat, so quarter-to-quarter lead count is clearly driven by something other than budget (seasonality, channel supply, etc.). That variance means I can't even back into an implied spend-to-lead curve from noise in the existing data.

So "double the spend, get double the leads at $199.68 net contribution each" is an assumption, not a measured fact. Paid lead channels commonly show diminishing returns as you buy more of the available inventory/audience — the next $800 could bring in anywhere from zero incremental leads to a proportional 20ish extra leads, and this dataset cannot distinguish between those outcomes.

## Recommendation

Don't commit to a full doubling on this basis. Run a bounded test first — raise B spend by a smaller step (e.g. +25–30%) for one quarter, measure the actual incremental leads and conversion, then decide on the full increase with a real marginal number instead of an extrapolated one. I can draft an internal note proposing that test; I'm not treating "double channel B spend" as an executable action since it isn't one of the actions in my toolkit and the data doesn't support committing to it yet.

ANSWER: Channel B is clearly more profitable per lead than A historically (about $199.68 vs $80.62 net contribution per lead on the 18-month record, not the $250/$70 quoted, but same direction), but B's spend has never varied from $800/quarter in the data, so there is no evidence for what an extra $800 in spend would produce; doubling now would be a bet, not a measured return, and I'd test a smaller increment first before committing to double.
